bib.title: The Elements of Statistical Learning, 2nd ed., Chapter 14: Unsupervised Learning

read.skipped: Figure plot glyphs (bullets, o marks, tick labels) were filtered out for reading; no prose skipped

question: What techniques (association rules, clustering, SOM, principal curves, spectral clustering, kernel and sparse PCA, NMF, ICA, MDS, nonlinear embeddings, PageRank) let one infer structure in Pr(X) without a response variable, and how do they relate?
contributions: A survey of the most common unsupervised learning techniques plus a few favoured by the authors, with worked examples on market-basket, microarray, digit, image, face, EEG and web-link data (section 14.1).

limits: No unsupervised method in the chapter has a direct measure of success: the authors say validity can only be argued heuristically and that this led to a proliferation of methods (section 14.1).

Most examples are small illustrations (toy 2-D/3-D simulations, 64 tumor samples, 658 digits); the chapter gives no benchmarks of clustering accuracy across methods and few numbers beyond the toy setups.
The ICA simulation (Fig 14.42) is reported only as a plot and a qualitative sentence; no Amari distances are printed.
Gap statistic, K-means and hierarchical methods are all heuristic about the number of clusters; the tumor data showed no clear kink and K=3 was picked for illustration.

Spectral clustering parameters (k, c, number of eigenvectors, number of clusters) must be chosen with no guidance beyond the toy example; eigenvalues of the toy do not clearly indicate how many eigenvectors to take.

Kernel PCA, NMF and local MDS are described as sensitive to kernel scale, starting values and tuning (tau, K) respectively; nonlinear dimension reduction is said to suit only high signal-to-noise data.

Dated (2009): sections on ICA/EEG, SOM/WEBSOM, ISOMAP/LLE and PageRank (original Google algorithm, d apparently 0.85) predate later practice; later methods (t-SNE, UMAP, deep clustering) are not covered. Software names (S-PLUS, Xgobi/GGobi, R ProDenICA, FastICA) are as of 2009.
Reference text equations are partly garbled in the PDF text layer, so formulas in this extraction are paraphrased, not verbatim.
practices: Association rules are only tractable for very large sparse binary data with a support threshold; low-support high-lift rules (vodka => caviar) will not be found. (p. 492)
For a rare item of interest, code only the presence dummy (e.g. income >= $40,000), not its absence, so rules target presence. (p. 495)

To get density/association structure with supervised tools, generate a reference sample (uniform, Gaussian with the same mean/covariance, or product of marginals by permuting each variable) at least as large as the data and classify data vs reference. (p. 497)

For generalized association rules use a rule learner (CART terminal nodes or PRIM) on the pooled data; PRIM is better for high-support, high-mean regions and gives control over the support/mean trade-off. (p. 499)
Clustering needs an explicit similarity notion from subject-matter knowledge; the choice of dissimilarity matters more than the algorithm. (p. 506)
Do not automatically standardize all features to equal influence for clustering; it can hide the groups (Fig 14.5). Weight variables by their relevance to separating groups. (p. 506)
For ordinal variables, replace M values by (i - 1/2)/M and treat as quantitative; for categorical variables use an explicit M x M loss matrix (default 0/1). (p. 504)
Handle missing values in dissimilarities by dropping the missing pairs, deleting objects with no shared values, imputing mean/median, or treating missing as a category. (p. 507)
Start K-means from many random initial means and keep the solution with the smallest objective; Hartigan-Wong guarantees no single switch improves it. (p. 510)
Use K-medoids when the data are only dissimilarities, when variables are not all quantitative, or when robustness to outliers is wanted, at higher computational cost. (p. 516)
Do not use cross-validation to pick K, because W_K keeps decreasing even on a test set; look for a kink in W_K or use the Gap statistic (also works when there is a single cluster). (p. 519)
Dendrograms impose hierarchy whether or not it exists; check with the cophenetic correlation and expect different linkages and small data changes to give different trees. (p. 522)

Prefer average linkage as a compromise between single (chaining) and complete (can violate closeness) linkage; it depends on the numeric scale of the dissimilarities whereas single and complete depend only on their order. (p. 525)
Check a SOM against K-means by comparing reconstruction error; it should not be much larger if the 2-D constraint is reasonable. With tiny neighbourhoods the SOM becomes online K-means. (p. 529)

Use spectral clustering rather than K-means for non-convex clusters; choose similarity graph type (mutual kNN or fully connected), k or kernel scale c, number of eigenvectors, and number of clusters. (p. 547)
Kernel PCA is sensitive to kernel scale and kernel nature, so tune c; for spectral clustering the nearest-neighbour truncation of the kernel matters. (p. 550)
Use sparse PCA (lasso-penalized loadings) when loadings need to be interpretable. (p. 550)
Treat NMF solutions with caution because they may be non-unique and depend on starting values. (p. 554)
Use ICA when sources are independent and non-Gaussian; whiten the data first (so A is orthogonal); use several random starts since the criteria are nonconvex. (p. 560)
Use nonlinear dimension reduction (ISOMAP, LLE, local MDS) only where signal-to-noise is very high; they are probably not as useful for observational data. (p. 572)

terms.definition: a set of N observations of a random p-vector X with joint density Pr(X); the goal is to directly infer the properties of this probability density without a teacher giving correct answers or error
the intersection of subsets of the p variables values, intersect_j (Xj in sj); if sj = Sj the variable does not appear in the rule
a subset K of the dummy variables; its support T(K) is the fraction of observations in which all of its dummies equal 1 (eq. 14.5)
C(A=>B) = T(A=>B)/T(A), an estimate of Pr(B | A) (eq. 14.8)
L(A=>B) = C(A=>B)/T(B), estimate of Pr(A and B)/Pr(A)Pr(B); expected confidence is T(B)
one pass per item-set size; candidates of size m need all size m-1 subsets frequent; relies on T(L) >= T(K) for L subset of K
N x N matrix D with d_ii' the dissimilarity (or similarity) between objects i and i'; most algorithms need nonnegative entries, zero diagonal and symmetry (use (D + D^T)/2)
assigns each observation to one of K clusters by a many-to-one map k = C(i), minimizing a loss such as W(C) = 1/2 sum_k sum_{C(i)=k} sum_{C(i')=k} d(xi, xi')
T = W(C) + B(C): total scatter is constant, so minimizing W(C) equals maximizing B(C)
alternately set each center to the mean of its assigned points and assign each point to the closest center, until assignments stop changing (Algorithm 14.1)
partitioning of space into regions of points closest to each centroid
image blocks as vectors are replaced by their nearest K-means centroid (codeword); the set of centroids is the codebook; rate is log2(K)/4 bits per pixel for 2x2 blocks with a fixed-length code
K-means with each cluster center restricted to be one of its observations, minimizing sum of dissimilarities to the center (Algorithm 14.2, eq. 14.35)
compares log W_K to its expectation under uniform data over a rectangle containing the data; K* = smallest K with G(K) >= G(K+1) - s'_{K+1} (eq. 14.39)
binary tree whose node heights equal the intergroup dissimilarity at merge, for hierarchical methods with the monotonicity property
correlation between the N(N-1)/2 input dissimilarities and the cophenetic dissimilarities C_ii' (the intergroup dissimilarity at which i and i' first join)
C_ii' <= max{C_ik, C_i'k} for cophenetic dissimilarities; triangles of all triples must be isosceles with the unequal side no longer than the equal sides
intergroup dissimilarity is the min (14.41), max (14.42) or mean (14.43) of the between-group pairwise dissimilarities
single linkage combining at low thresholds observations linked by a series of close intermediate observations; produces clusters with very large diameter
constrained K-means in which prototypes lie on a 1-D or 2-D grid manifold; online update m_k <- m_k + alpha (x_i - m_k) for neighbours of the closest prototype (eq. 14.46)
f(lambda) = E(X | lambda_f(X) = lambda): each point on the curve is the average of all data points that project to it (eq. 14.61)
the k points minimizing expected distance from X to its closest prototype; distributional analogs of K-means centroids

minimum over translation and rotation of ||X2 - (X1 R + 1 mu^T)||_F, with R = U V^T from SVD of X1~^T X2~; the Procrustes average finds the shape M closest to all shapes in squared Procrustes distance
L = G - W (unnormalized), with W the adjacency matrix of edge weights and G diagonal of vertex degrees; normalized version I - G^-1 W
PCA on the double-centered kernel (gram) matrix K~ = (I - M) K (I - M) = U D^2 U^T with Z = UD, mimicking PCA in a nonlinearly expanded feature space

code.snippet: K-means (Algorithm 14.1): 1. given assignment C, set each m_k to the mean of its cluster; 2. given means, C(i) = argmin_{1<=k<=K} ||x_i - m_k||^2; 3. repeat until assignments do not change. Minimizes sum_k sum_{C(i)=k} ||x_i - m_k||^2 (14.33).
K-medoids (Algorithm 14.2): 1. for each cluster, i*_k = argmin over {i : C(i)=k} of sum_{C(i')=k} D(x_i, x_i'); m_k = x_{i*_k}; 2. C(i) = argmin_k D(x_i, m_k); 3. iterate until no change.
Unsupervised as supervised: mu(x) = E(Y|x) = g(x)/(g(x)+g0(x)); g-hat(x) = g0(x) * mu-hat(x)/(1 - mu-hat(x)) (14.12); f(x) = log g(x)/g0(x), g-hat(x) = g0(x) e^{f(x)} (14.14).
support T(A=>B) = T(K); confidence C(A=>B) = T(A=>B)/T(A) (14.8); lift L(A=>B) = C(A=>B)/T(B).
PageRank: p_i = (1-d) + d * sum_j (L_ij / c_j) p_j (14.107); power iteration p_k <- A p_{k-1}; p_k <- N p_k / (e^T p_k) (14.110); d = 0.85.
Spectral clustering: s_ii' = exp(-d_ii'^2 / c); L = G - W (14.63); take the m eigenvectors of L for the m smallest eigenvalues (dropping the trivial constant one) and run K-means on the rows.

ProDenICA (Algorithm 14.3): 1. initialize A (random Gaussian matrix, orthogonalized); 2. alternate until A converges: (a) given A, fit each g_j by penalized (spline) density estimation; (b) given g_j, one fixed-point step a_j <- E[X g_j'(a_j^T X)] - E[g_j''(a_j^T X)] a_j, then A <- U V^T from SVD of A.
